1. The animation shows a historical comparison of buying and renting in the US. It uses FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. Each tile in the grid is one possible start month, from January 1991 on, and 247 start months are shown. A lit tile means the buyer was ahead after the holding period. A dark tile means the renter was ahead. The labels say "illustrative" and "history, not a forecast."

2. The holding period changes. At 15 years, every start month (100%) is lit, and the weakest case still has the buyer $79,829 ahead. Under "held ten years," a block of tiles in the middle turns dark, so the renter came out ahead for those start months. Under "held fifteen years," the grid is all lit again. The last two frames switch to a character, Nina, standing between an apartment and a house. The label first reads "how long Nina stays: unknown," then "the rent tag: unchanged."

3. Historically, buying beat renting in every start month when the home was held 15 years. At ten years, buying mostly won, but some start months favored renting. So the result depends on how long you stay. Nina's case shows that her own stay length is unknown, so the historical record can't settle her choice. The "rent tag: unchanged" label suggests the rent comparison stays fixed while the buying outcome depends on time.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer could take away that buying has historically paid off over long holding periods, and that staying a shorter time carries more risk. The "not a forecast" label cautions against treating this as a guarantee.

5. The advice in 4 is my own reading. The on-screen text only reports the results (100% lit, weakest case $79,829 ahead, some dark tiles at ten years) and says "unknown" about Nina's stay. It never tells the viewer to buy or rent.
